facts.t: Ordinary Lok Adalats cannot decide anything
facts.d: State of Punjab v. Jalour Singh is explicit — an award may rest only on a compromise. Permanent Lok Adalats are the sole exception, holding genuine decision-making power over public utility disputes.

facts.t: Jharkhand cleared 99.95% of its listed cases in one sitting
facts.d: That was the first National Lok Adalat of 2025. The method was unglamorous: strong coordination by the State Legal Services Authority and pre-identification of cases already ripe for settlement.

facts.t: Nobody tracks whether the money is actually paid
facts.d: Disposal figures are published in crores of cases, but there is almost no granular data on post-settlement compliance. A settled case and a satisfied claimant are not the same thing.

bank.q: Which case held that a Lok Adalat may pass an award only on the basis of a compromise?
o: P. T. Thomas v. Thomas Job
State of Punjab v. Jalour Singh
bank.e: Jalour Singh (2008) — no power to adjudicate on merits. P. T. Thomas (2005) held the award to be as good as a civil court decree.

bank.q: Comparing Lok Adalats with Permanent Lok Adalats, consider the following:
s: Ordinary Lok Adalats handle both pre-litigation and pending cases.
If no settlement is reached, an ordinary Lok Adalat returns the case to court.
A Permanent Lok Adalat may decide the matter on merits, except where an offence is involved.
bank.e: All three are correct — the decisive difference being the Permanent Lok Adalat's adjudicatory power.

bank.q: Which one of the following can NOT be taken up by a Lok Adalat?
o: Dowry death and certain POCSO matters
bank.e: Offences against women and children where compromise is disallowed fall outside, along with non-compoundable offences generally.

bank.as: Lok Adalats are criticised as producing assembly-line justice.
bank.rs: Pressure to clear crores of cases in a single sitting can compromise scrutiny of consent and fairness.
bank.e: Both true and the Reason explains the Assertion — hence the proposal for cooling-off periods in high-value or vulnerable-party settlements.

bank.q: Consider the following concerns about voluntariness:
s: Weaker parties may accept lower amounts to avoid prolonged litigation.
Claimants against insurers and banks face unequal bargaining power.
Section 21 provides a statutory right of appeal against a Lok Adalat award.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Section 21 bars appeal — only a narrow writ remedy survives.

bank.q: Match List I (country) with List II (ADR practice):
pairs: 1. Community-embedded resolution centres integrated with formal courts
2. Court-annexed mediation with trained professionals and strict timelines
3. Judicially mandated ADR referral with strong small-claims infrastructure
4. Lok Adalats with awards deemed civil court decrees
bank.e: Singapore's professional court-annexed mediation, America's mandated ADR and small claims, South Africa's community centres, and India's Lok Adalats.

bank.q: All of the following are Indian best practices EXCEPT:
o: National Lok Adalats on fixed dates, often themed by subject
Virtual and e-Lok Adalats retained after the pandemic
The Legal Aid Defence Counsel System professionalising panels
Mandatory referral of all pending civil suits to Lok Adalat
bank.e: Referral depends on party agreement or the court's assessment of suitability — there is no blanket mandate.

bank.q: Which categories dominate Lok Adalat disposals, raising the bulk-clearance concern?
o: Cheque bounce, MACT and bank recovery
bank.e: Semi-mechanical and often undefended categories, which is why critics question whether volume equals substantive resolution.

bank.q: With reference to proposed solutions, consider the following:
s: A NALSA-led compliance tracker measuring real rather than paper resolution.
Publishing case-category-wise data rather than aggregate disposal figures.
Removing the finality of Lok Adalat awards to allow ordinary appeals.
bank.e: Statements 1 and 2 are proposed. Finality is preserved — the remedy sought is better consent safeguards before the award, not appeal after it.

bank.q: Permanent Lok Adalats deal exclusively with disputes concerning:
bank.e: Transport, postal, electricity, water, hospitals and insurance — within prescribed pecuniary limits.
